title: Brigid of Kildare
hookLine: an Irish abbess famed for giving away everything, even her father's sword

lines: A FATHER FED UP WITH GIVING.
cards: Food from the house, butter from the kitchen: a girl keeps giving her father's things away to anyone poor who asks, and he's had enough.
He drives her to a king's hall to sell her, and goes inside, leaving his sword in the chariot. While he's in there, a poor man comes by and asks for help. The girl has nothing of her own.
So she hands him her father's sword. Her name is Brigid.

teach.b: That's the story as the old Lives of Brigid tell it, and it's worth being plain about what those are. They aren't diaries.

They're Lives written by monks, Cogitosus among them, after her time, gathering what Ireland remembered and loved about her. Read that way, they're a portrait, and nearly every brushstroke is the same color: she gives.
When her father finds the sword gone, he's furious, and the king asks the girl why she gives away her father's goods.

teach.h: IF I HAD THE KING'S TREASURE.
teach.b: Brigid answers, in the story, that if she had the king's whole treasure, she would give it all to Christ, through the poor. And the king lets her go. A girl like that, he decides, is not one to keep.
She becomes a nun, and an abbess.
The Lives tell of her church at Kildare, a community of women and men, of guests fed, butter that didn't run out, and a table kept open. Irish tradition gives her a striking title: Mary of the Gael.
Mary, the mother of Jesus, for the Irish: a mother to them, close and generous. Behind the stories stand lines from the Gospels.

teach.h: GIVE TO HIM THAT ASKETH THEE.
teach.b: Jesus says, in the King James: "Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away." And in Acts, Paul recalls a saying of Jesus: "It is more blessed to give than to receive."
Brigid's stories take those lines as far as they will go. Not the spare coat. The father's sword.
Some readers smile at the miracles in the Lives; others treasure them. Either way the picture holds: a woman whose hands kept opening.

how: Catholic, Anglican and Orthodox Christians honor Brigid as a saint, and in Ireland people weave Brigid's crosses from rushes around her feast day.

games.q: your father is inside the king's hall. a poor man asks you for help. you have nothing of your own, but your father's sword is lying in the chariot. what do you do?
o: tell him you have nothing to give.
games.why: Brigid gives him the sword. when the king asks why, she says she'd give the king's whole treasure to Christ through the poor.

practice: Look, in your mind, around the place you live, past the junk drawer, for something you actually use: a good coat, a tool, a book you love, a free afternoon.
Picture who could use it, a neighbor, a shelter, a friend starting over, and notice what happens in you as you imagine handing it over. If you pray, offer it to God before you offer it to them.
